newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces more than three weeks out of Kremlin.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces more than three weeks out of Kremlin.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin made no significant improvement on Friday in his battle in hospital with pneumonia and doctors said he should not return to the Kremlin for more than three weeks.

Doctors said the 65-year-old president was breathing more easily. But the chief Kremlin doctor said Yeltsin was depressed by his latest setback, two weeks after returning to his Kremlin office following a near six-month absence for heart surgery.
Yeltsin's illness prompted some Russian newspapers to draw gloomy conclusions about the country's political health and said it could mean further delays in badly-needed reforms.

"The president is breathing with more ease, there are less crepitations in his lungs. The temperature remains normal, blood pressure is stable," a Kremlin statement said after doctors examined Yeltsin at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital.
"But at the same time doctors think it is too early to speak about a breakthrough."

Sergei Mironov, the head of the Kremlin medical centre, said Yeltsin should spend three more days in hospital and about three weeks recovering before returning to the Kremlin, although the president was resisting doctors' advice.
"Of course this is depressing him, of course his mood is not a very happy one but I see no reason for particular pessimism," Mironov told reporters.

A Kremlin spokeswoman declined to comment on a report on the Ekho Moskvy radio station in Moscow which quoted hospital sources as saying Yeltsin was suffering from an inflammation "of medium gravity" of both lungs.

Yeltsin, who had a major heart operation on November 5, was taken to hospital on Wednesday with what the Kremlin initially described as the first signs of pneumonia. It described his condition as pneumonia on Thursday but gave few details.

Russian financial markets shrugged off Yeltsin's illness. Leading shares soared to record levels on heavy volume as foreign investors poured money into Russia and some stocks rose by more than 10 percent during the day.
But some newspapers said the vast nuclear state of nearly 150 million people was leaderless.
"President Sick, Premier On Holiday, Country All On Its Own", the liberal newspaper Izvestia said in a headline.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta said officials were unable to lead without a healthy president and that the country was much sicker than the president.

"It's completely clear that if the situation does not change for the better in the near future, then an already weakened Russia will suffer additional losses in domestic, and especially, foreign policy," it said.
The Kremlin has portrayed Yeltsin as still engaged in state affairs. It said on Thursday that he was in contact by telephone with a number of Russian and foreign leaders.
Kremlin officials have also played down his condition and say it has nothing to do with last November's quintuple heart bypass operation.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional deputy, was confident enough to begin a planned week's holiday near Moscow. He spoke by telephone to Yeltsin, who is being treated with antibiotics.

Chernomyrdin, who would assume power for up to three months before elections if the president were to step down, spent six months effectively running the country after Yeltsin suffered a bout of heart trouble shortly before his re-election on July 3.
Yeltsin has a busy schedule of meetings with foreign leaders in the next few months. Mironov said the schedule could be amended but gave no details.

A summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), which Yeltsin had been due to attend, was postponed from January 19 until January 30-31. Officials said the decision was not taken because of Yeltsin's health.
